gbs333-aa4354-d1e107.summary: States the question: whether an attribute (passio) knowable in a science properly so called is really distinct from its subject.

gbs333-aa4354-d1e118.summary: Introductory notabile. Notes that some treat this question, with the preceding one, as an appendix to the first principal question, but Biel is indifferent to its status since it stands third in order. After recalling and rejecting the opinion that every attribute is really identical with its subject, he distinguishes two senses of 'passio': real, for a thing that belongs to another, i.e., an inhering form; and logical, for a term accidentally predicable of another.
claims: Whether this is a principal question or an appendix is immaterial.
The view that every attribute is really identical with its subject is to be rejected.
'Passio' is taken really for an inhering form and logically for a term accidentally predicable of another.

gbs333-aa4354-d1e165.summary: First conclusion: a real attribute is distinct from its subject, because every inhering form, accidental or substantial, is distinct from the subject in which it inheres, and a real attribute is such a form.
claims: A real attribute is distinct from its subject.
Every inhering form, accidental or substantial, is distinct from its subject of inherence.

gbs333-aa4354-d1e178.summary: Second conclusion: every logical attribute is distinct from its subject, since such a term connotes something beyond its subject and is predicated of it, and subject and predicate are not the same term.
claims: Every logical attribute is distinct from its subject.
A logical attribute connotes something beyond its subject.
concepts: distinction of subject and predicate terms

gbs333-aa4354-d1e202.summary: Third conclusion, generalizing the first two: nothing that is in another is the same as that in which it is, whether 'being in' means real inherence or affirmative predication.
claims: Nothing that is in another is identical with that in which it is, whether by real inherence or by affirmative predication.

gbs333-aa4354-d1e215.summary: Fourth conclusion: since both real and logical attributes are distinct from their subjects, they are separable from them. Yet a logical attribute is sometimes called inseparable in the sense that it can never be truly denied of a subject that is convertible with it and has supposition.
claims: Both real and logical attributes are separable from their subjects.
A logical attribute is called inseparable only in that it can never be truly denied of an existing convertible subject.

gbs333-aa4354-d1e235.summary: Explains how attribute and subject are distinct at each level of language. Spoken and written terms ('risible' and 'man') are really distinct. For mental terms the answer depends on the theory of concepts: if a concept has subjective being in the mind as a real quality, attribute and subject concepts are really distinct; if a concept has only objective being (a fictum), they are distinct by reason only, being rationes rather than things, and so neither really distinct nor really the same.
claims: Spoken and written attribute-terms are really distinct from their subject-terms.
If concepts have subjective being in the mind, mental attribute and subject are really distinct.
If concepts have only objective being, they are distinct only by reason, being neither really distinct nor really identical.

gbs333-aa4354-d1e268.summary: Begins a clarifying excursus on abstract terms: an abstract term principally signifies that by which a concrete denomination belongs to a thing, as heat signifies that by which something is called hot, and likewise whiteness, risibility, similarity, humanity, corporeity, and blindness.
claims: An abstract term principally signifies that by which a thing receives the corresponding concrete denomination.

gbs333-aa4354-d1e293.summary: Begins a survey of the ways a thing is denominated, from intrinsic and extrinsic, existing and non-existing sources. First, a thing is denominated by reason of its own essence, by absolute names such as genera, species, and individuals in the category of substance; their abstracts are synonymous with their concretes (e.g. 'man' and 'humanity' taken absolutely), corresponding to the same mental concept despite their different spoken form.
claims: Things are denominated in many ways, from intrinsic and extrinsic, existent and non-existent sources.
Denominations from a thing's essence are typically absolute names of substances.
Abstract and concrete substance terms such as 'man' and 'humanity', taken absolutely, are synonyms corresponding to a single concept.

gbs333-aa4354-d1e337.summary: Second mode of denomination: from an essential part, as man is called rational from the rational soul or material from matter. The abstract ('rationality') then signifies that part, absolutely or connotatively as part of man, and is not synonymous with the concrete, because 'rational' supposits for the whole man and 'rationality' only for the soul.
claims: A thing can be denominated from an essential part, e.g. 'rational' from the rational soul.
In that case the abstract term supposits only for the part, not the whole, and is not synonymous with the concrete.

gbs333-aa4354-d1e370.summary: Third mode: a substance is denominated from an absolute accidental form inhering in it, as white from whiteness, virtuous from virtue, just from justice, knowing from knowledge. Such abstracts are sometimes taken absolutely, signifying the accidental form alone; any absolute (non-relative) thing can be signified absolutely.
claims: A substance can be denominated from an absolute accidental form inhering in it.
Abstracts of such forms can be taken absolutely, signifying only the form.
Any absolute (non-relational) thing can be signified absolutely.

gbs333-aa4354-d1e399.summary: Adds that such abstracts can also be taken connotatively, signifying the accidental forms as inhering in their subject.
claims: Abstracts of accidental forms can be taken connotatively, as signifying the forms' inherence in a subject.

gbs333-aa4354-d1e410.summary: Fourth mode: a thing is denominated from a motion, action, or passion (mobile, risible, tractable, passible), and the abstract then signifies the motion or act, either with an aptitude for it or as actual.
claims: A thing can be denominated from a motion, action, or passion.
The corresponding abstract signifies the motion or act, either as aptitude or as actual.

gbs333-aa4354-d1e426.summary: Fifth and sixth modes: a thing can be denominated from something wholly extrinsic, even distant in place and subject, as in 'heat-producing' and 'creative' (named from effects in another), 'clothed', 'right', 'left', 'distant', 'located'; or from something that does not exist, i.e., a lack, as in 'blind', 'deaf', 'non-man', 'incorruptible', which include a negation. In all cases the abstract signifies that from which the thing is denominated.
claims: A thing can be denominated from something wholly extrinsic, such as an effect produced in another.
A thing can be denominated from a privation or non-existent, and such denominations include a negation.
In every case the abstract signifies that from which the denomination is taken.

gbs333-aa4354-d1e469.summary: Asks what an abstract term supposits for: when the concrete denomination is taken precisely from one thing, the abstract supposits for that thing, as 'whiteness' and 'heat' do.
claims: When a concrete denomination derives from exactly one thing, the abstract supposits for that thing.

gbs333-aa4354-d1e485.summary: When the denomination derives from several things, the abstract supposits not for any one of them but for all together and for none separately, e.g. 'risibility' supposits jointly for the power of laughing (really the soul) and the act of laughing, which are related as cause and effect. Alternatively, if one of the several is principal and ordered to the others, the abstract can supposit for it and connote the others, so that 'risibility' supposits for the man or soul while connoting the aptitude to laugh.
claims: When a denomination is taken from several things, the abstract supposits for all jointly and none separately.
The power to laugh is really the soul.
If one of several is principal, the abstract may supposit for it and connote the others; thus 'risibility' supposits for the soul or man and connotes the ability to laugh.

gbs333-aa4354-d1e524.summary: Draws a corollary for 'what is it?' questions about abstract terms: in general, the right answer to 'what is X?' is to state that for which the term X supposits.
claims: The correct answer to 'what is X?' is to give what the term X supposits for.

gbs333-aa4354-d1e537.summary: An abstract term including a negation, such as 'blindness', supposits for nothing in an affirmative proposition, since it signifies not something's being but its absence; hence blindness is nothing. To the objection that 'blindness is a privation' is a true affirmative, so that its terms must supposit, Biel replies that this is true only when the copula expresses signified rather than exercised act, meaning 'blindness signifies a privation', with 'blindness' in material supposition for the term. Taken as asserting real existence of the extremes, the proposition is false, since blindness is nothing.
claims: Abstract privative terms such as 'blindness' supposit for nothing in affirmative propositions.
Blindness is nothing.
'Blindness is a privation' is true only with the copula taken as actus signatus, the subject in material supposition.
Taken as asserting the real existence of its terms, 'blindness is a privation' is false.

gbs333-aa4354-d1e581.summary: Suggests that the same answer might be extended to all connotative abstract terms: perhaps none supposits personally for anything. The author (Ockham) touches on this approach later, in distinction 5, question 1.
claims: Perhaps no connotative abstract term supposits personally for anything.

gbs333-aa4354.summary: Quaestio 3 asks whether a scientifically knowable attribute is really distinct from its subject. Rejecting the view that attributes are really identical with their subjects, Biel distinguishes real attributes (inhering forms) from logical ones (terms accidentally predicable) and concludes that both are distinct from their subjects and separable from them, since nothing that is in another, by inherence or by predication, is identical with it; a logical attribute is 'inseparable' only in that it cannot truly be denied of an existing convertible subject. The kind of distinction depends on the level of language: spoken and written terms are really distinct, while mental terms are really distinct only if concepts are real qualities and merely distinct by reason if they are ficta. Most of the question is an Ockhamist excursus on abstract terms. They signify that from which a concrete denomination is taken, which may be the essence (where abstract and concrete are synonyms), an essential part, an absolute accident, a motion or act, something extrinsic, or a privation. The excursus then sets out what such abstracts supposit for: one thing, several jointly, or a principal significate with connotation. Privative abstracts like 'blindness' supposit for nothing, so 'blindness is a privation' is true only as a signified act in material supposition, and perhaps every connotative abstract lacks personal supposition.
claims: Every attribute, real or logical, is distinct from and separable from its subject.
Whether mental attributes are really or only rationally distinct from their subjects depends on whether concepts are real qualities or ficta.
Abstract terms signify that from which the concrete denomination is taken; abstract and concrete substance terms are synonymous.
Privative abstract terms such as 'blindness' supposit for nothing; blindness is nothing.
concepts: esse subiectivum vs. obiectivum of concepts
